newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's new electricity market heralds new era - EMCO.
newsitem.headline: NZ's new electricity market heralds new era - EMCO.

text.p: New Zealand's new electricity market, which becomes fully operational on October 1, will herald a new era of power pricing in which consumers also have a say, Electricity Market Company (EMCO) chief executive Lincoln Gould said on Wednesday.
"For the first time consumers will be involved in establishing the price and will not any longer be held in the stranglehold of being just price takers," Gould told a briefing of journalists.

"It is really the opportunity for efficient pricing to come into the market which is the big advantage that will occur. And those advantages ought to be deliverable to the domestic consumers, they shouldn't just lie with the retailing distributors," he said.
In the new wholesale market, prices will be determined on the basis of the equilibrium between supply and demand, in contrast to the cost-based methods of the past.

A central aim of the market is to give economic efficiency signals indicating where the next generation plant should be built and to foster competition between all market participants. "The risks associated with building generation and building new transmission plants are certainly real," Gould said.
"This market has been designed so that risks will lie where they fall, and it will be those organisations that are best able to manage commercial risk that will survive."
He said some companies may well go bankrupt in the new market place.

"We may in fact see financial failure, we may see bankruptcy, but we shouldn't worry about that. The lights will stay on, and it will be a case of those who are best able to be efficient in the way they service their customers and manage the risks associated with that, that will survive."

Critics of the new market have been quick to point out that under the market rules, the potential exists for dominant players to push up the price of electricity above a competitive level, otherwise known as "gaming".

There are fears that Electricity Corporation of New Zealand (ECNZ), which contributes around 70 percent of the country's total generation, and Contact Energy with just less than 30 percent, will act unilaterally to game the market.
Gould acknowledged that the opportunity for dominant behaviour existed, but said the market was built so that actions were very transparent.
"The Market Surveillance Committee has extremely wide powers to deal with breaches of the rules," he said.
Actions against participants for "anti-social" behaviour included sanctions such as fines and disbarment.

Gould said one of the key advantages of the new market was that the industry had designed it. "The industry hasn't had something imposed on them. So we think we've got a much more flexible market which will be more in tune with consumer demands than if it had been imposed by some government legislation."
Gould said the new market was "a major step" after many smaller ones which would see a full, open commodity market for electricity established in New Zealand.
